name: Parietal lobe
func: The upper-middle part of each hemisphere. It processes touch and body position, combines senses to build a map of the space around you, and guides reaching. The left side also helps with reading, writing and math.

levels.kid:
The **parietal lobe** sits on the top and back of your head, like where a crown would go.

It is your brain's **map maker**. It knows where your hands and feet are even when your eyes are closed. Try it: close your eyes and touch your nose. Your parietal lobe helped!

It also mixes what you see and feel so you can reach out and grab a cup without knocking it over.

The left parietal lobe helps with numbers and letters, like counting your toys and writing your name. The right one helps you notice everything around you, on both sides of the room.
levels.hs:
The **parietal lobe** lies behind the frontal lobe and above the temporal lobe. Its borders are the **central sulcus** in front, the **lateral fissure** below (separating it from the temporal lobe), and the **parieto-occipital sulcus** behind, which is easiest to see on the medial surface where it divides it from the occipital lobe. On the outer surface, the boundary with the occipital and temporal lobes is just an imaginary line.

It has three main parts:

- The **postcentral gyrus** at the front, the primary somatosensory cortex for touch and body position.
- The **superior parietal lobule** on top, which builds a sense of where your body is in space and guides reaching and grasping.
- The **inferior parietal lobule** below, made of the **supramarginal gyrus** (curving around the end of the lateral fissure) and the **angular gyrus** (curving around the end of the superior temporal sulcus).

The two sides do different jobs. The **left (dominant) parietal lobe** supports language-linked skills such as reading, writing, arithmetic and telling left from right. The **right parietal lobe** dominates spatial attention to both sides of space. That is why damage to the right parietal lobe can make someone ignore the entire left side of their world, a condition called **neglect**.
levels.college:
The intraparietal sulcus divides the superior parietal lobule (Brodmann 5 and 7) from the inferior parietal lobule (supramarginal gyrus, BA 40; angular gyrus, BA 39). On the medial surface, the **precuneus** lies between the paracentral lobule and the parieto-occipital sulcus.

Functions by region:

- **Posterior parietal cortex** sits in the **dorsal visual stream**, the "where/how" pathway described by Ungerleider and Mishkin and reframed by Goodale and Milner. It converts what you see into body-centered coordinates for action.
- The **intraparietal sulcus** contains areas that code eye movements (LIP), reaching (MIP, the "parietal reach region") and grasping (AIP), and it is central to number sense.
- The **left supramarginal gyrus** supports phonological processing and skilled-movement plans (praxis); the **left angular gyrus** links written words to their meaning and sounds.
- The **precuneus** is a hub of the **default mode network**, active during self-reflection and memory recall.

Connections: the superior longitudinal fasciculus links parietal to frontal cortex (the dorsal attention network), and the arcuate fasciculus passes beneath the supramarginal gyrus between Wernicke's and Broca's areas. Thalamic input comes from the pulvinar and lateral posterior nucleus.

Blood supply: the **MCA** supplies most of the lateral surface, the **ACA** the medial surface in front of the precuneus, and the **posterior cerebral artery** part of the posterior medial region. The parieto-occipital region is a watershed zone between the MCA and PCA, vulnerable when blood pressure drops.
levels.phd:
Parietal neurons transform sensory signals between reference frames. Recordings in monkeys showed that many posterior parietal neurons have retina-centered receptive fields whose firing is scaled by eye position, called **gain fields** (Andersen and Zipser). A network reading many gain-modulated neurons can compute where an object is relative to the head or body, which is exactly what you need to reach for something you saw.

Area **LIP** contains a **priority map**: neurons fire for objects that are salient or relevant to the current goal, regardless of the motor response. During perceptual decisions, LIP activity ramps up as evidence accumulates toward a choice, matching drift-diffusion models of decision-making (Shadlen and Newsome). Whether LIP causally computes the decision is debated, because inactivating it in some studies barely changes choices.

Parietal cortex is also important for **body ownership**. In the **rubber hand illusion**, synchronous stroking of a seen fake hand and the hidden real hand makes the fake hand feel like one's own, with activity in premotor and intraparietal regions.

Hemispheric asymmetry of attention has several proposed explanations. Kinsbourne argued that each hemisphere pushes attention to the opposite side, with the left hemisphere's push stronger. Mesulam proposed that the right hemisphere attends to both sides of space while the left attends mainly to the right. Corbetta's model separates a bilateral **dorsal attention network** (intraparietal sulcus and frontal eye fields) from a right-lateralized **ventral network** (temporoparietal junction and ventral frontal cortex), and suggests neglect arises when ventral damage unbalances the dorsal network.

Numerical cognition maps onto the horizontal intraparietal sulcus, where neurons in monkeys are tuned to specific quantities.
levels.expert:
Parietal syndromes are heavily exam-driven:

**Non-dominant (usually right) parietal lesions:**
- **Hemispatial neglect** of the left side: the patient eats only the right half of the plate, bisects lines to the right of center, and draws a clock with all the numbers crammed on the right.
- **Anosognosia:** unawareness of their own left-sided weakness.
- **Sensory and visual extinction** to double simultaneous stimulation.
- Dressing apraxia and constructional apraxia.

**Dominant (usually left) parietal lesions:**
- **Gerstmann syndrome** (angular gyrus): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion.
- **Ideomotor apraxia:** cannot perform a learned gesture on command (e.g., "show me how you brush your teeth") despite normal strength.
- Alexia with agraphia; conduction aphasia from lesions affecting the supramarginal gyrus and arcuate fasciculus.

**Bilateral parieto-occipital lesions:** **Balint syndrome**, with simultanagnosia (seeing one object at a time), optic ataxia (misreaching under visual guidance) and ocular apraxia. Causes include watershed infarcts after cardiac arrest and **posterior cortical atrophy**, a visual variant of Alzheimer disease.

**Any parietal lesion** can cause cortical sensory loss and a contralateral **inferior quadrantanopia** ("pie on the floor") from damage to the upper optic radiations passing deep in the lobe.

**Imaging:** MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging confirms stroke. The precuneus and posterior cingulate show early reduced metabolism on FDG-PET in Alzheimer disease.

**Surgery:** parietal approaches reach the atrium of the lateral ventricle and deep tumors. The superior parietal lobule is a common corridor because it is relatively safe compared with the dominant inferior parietal lobule, where language and praxis are mapped with awake techniques. Neglect usually improves over weeks to months, helped by rehabilitation such as prism adaptation.

keyPoints: Borders: central sulcus, lateral fissure, parieto-occipital sulcus
Parts: postcentral gyrus, superior and inferior parietal lobules (supramarginal + angular)
Right lesion → left neglect and anosognosia
Left angular gyrus lesion → Gerstmann syndrome
Optic radiation damage → contralateral inferior quadrantanopia

test.q: A patient after a right parietal stroke shaves only the right side of his face. This is:
test.explain: Right parietal lesions cause left-sided neglect.

test.q: Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion together form ______ syndrome.
test.explain: Gerstmann syndrome localizes to the dominant angular gyrus.

test.q: Which gyrus curves around the end of the lateral fissure?
test.explain: The supramarginal gyrus caps the posterior end of the lateral fissure; the angular gyrus caps the superior temporal sulcus.

test.q: A parietal lobe lesion damaging the optic radiations causes which visual field defect?
test.explain: Parietal fibers carry the lower visual field ('pie on the floor').

test.q: Unawareness of one's own paralysis after a right parietal stroke is called ______.
test.explain: Anosognosia is common with non-dominant parietal lesions.

test.q: Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia form which syndrome?
test.explain: Balint syndrome comes from bilateral parieto-occipital damage.
